title: Byproduct Founder
opening: A useful result can outlive the investigation that produced it. Decide what helps the pursuit, what another person can do with the result, and what continuing work would actually require.

labels.mapIntro: Choose a decision to inspect. A byproduct can be shared, offered, maintained, or left alone; usefulness does not prove a business.
labels.recipientIntro: Name a person or group with a real need. An audience is a possible recipient, not evidence that anyone has acted or paid.
labels.contact: What contact lets them inspect or try the result?
labels.vessel: What must continue without daily creator labor?
labels.sourceQuote: A vessel is the structure that lets the work continue beyond its creator's daily involvement. It can contain the method, tools, people, resources and decision rules needed to reproduce and improve the result. The governing standards have to survive delegation and succession too.
labels.practice: Apply this to a real result
labels.practiceIntro: Keep the pursuit and a possible offering distinct. Describe what another person could do, what you have observed, and what continuation would require.

steps.title: Keep the pursuit in charge
steps.detail: Name the question and worthy work already under way. A product plan should serve that aim; if it does not, choose it explicitly as a separate pursuit.

steps.title: Make the useful result inspectable
steps.detail: Show the result through a demonstration, explanation, or an appropriate chance to try it. A story about usefulness is not observed use.

steps.title: Observe what a recipient can do
steps.detail: Name a particular recipient and the capability the result may supply. Distinguish a possible audience from someone who has tried it and from evidence of benefit.

steps.title: Choose an honest offer, if any
steps.detail: An offer describes a real exchange. Interest, a demonstration, a purchase, successful delivery, and continuing economics answer different questions.

steps.title: Set gates that protect the work
steps.detail: State what access or commitment is limited, why, and what the gate protects: attention, quality, rights, or working conditions. Do not make an unsupported promise.

steps.title: Arrange a continuing vessel when justified
steps.detail: Name methods, tools, people, resources, and decision rules that can reproduce and maintain the result beyond daily creator labor. A vessel requires real operators and resources; it does not guarantee success.

contactTypes.label: Read or hear an explanation
contactTypes.detail: Makes the relationship inspectable; it does not show that the recipient can use it.

contactTypes.label: Watch a demonstration
contactTypes.detail: Shows a result under stated conditions; it does not establish demand or repeatability.

contactTypes.label: Try the result
contactTypes.detail: Can reveal what a recipient does with it. Record the conditions and what you actually observed.

fields.label: What question or pursuit should stay in charge?
Who could use the result, and what could they do?
What did a recipient actually inspect, try, or do?
What offer or access gate, if any, protects the work?
What people, methods, tools, resources, and rules would continue it?

example.pursuit: Investigate how to prepare a reliable meal with limited equipment.
example.recipient: A neighbor with the same equipment might use a tested preparation method.
example.evidence: They read the recipe and prepared one meal in their own kitchen. One attempt does not establish broad demand or repeatability.
example.offer: Sharing the recipe may be enough. A prepared product would need an honest price, rights, safe production, and a real delivery plan.
example.return: If prepared meals are pursued, identify an operator, equipment, ingredients, quality checks, resources, and decisions for changing or stopping production.
